questions.q: In the standard anatomical position, how do the palms of the hands face?
questions.explain: In the standard anatomical position, the body stands upright facing forward with the upper limbs at the sides and the palms facing anteriorly. Facing posteriorly occurs during pronation.

open.q: In the standard anatomical position, what direction do the palms of the hands face?

questions.q: In the standard anatomical position, which direction do the toes point?
questions.explain: In the standard anatomical position, the feet are slightly apart with the toes pointing anteriorly. Lateral or medial rotation of the lower limb shifts the direction the toes point.

open.q: In the standard anatomical position, what direction do the toes point?

questions.q: Which vertical plane passes longitudinally through the midline of the body to divide it into equal right and left halves?
questions.explain: The median (midsagittal) plane passes through the center of the body to create equal left and right halves. Parasagittal planes are parallel to the median plane but off-center.

open.q: Which vertical plane passes longitudinally through the midline of the body to divide it into equal right and left halves?

questions.q: Which plane divides the body or an organ into anterior and posterior portions?
questions.explain: The coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane oriented at right angles to the median plane that separates anterior from posterior parts. Transverse planes divide superior from inferior parts.

open.q: Which anatomical plane divides the body or an organ into anterior and posterior portions?

questions.q: A vertical plane passes parallel to the median plane, dividing the right half of the chest into unequal medial and lateral parts. What is this plane called?
questions.explain: Any vertical plane parallel to the median plane that is not on the midline is a parasagittal plane. Coronal planes run side-to-side, and axial planes are horizontal.

open.q: What is a vertical plane that lies parallel to the median plane and divides the body into unequal right and left parts?

questions.q: Which directional term describes a position closer to the point of attachment of a limb to the trunk?
questions.explain: Proximal indicates greater proximity to the trunk or point of origin of a limb, whereas distal indicates greater distance from that attachment point.

open.q: Which directional term refers to a location closer to the trunk or point of attachment of a limb?

questions.q: Which directional term means closer to the median plane of the body?
questions.explain: Medial means nearer to the median plane, while lateral means farther away from the median plane. External and internal describe positions relative to the center of an organ or cavity.

open.q: Which directional term means closer to the median plane of the body?

questions.q: Which pair of terms is most commonly used to describe positions on the dorsum or palm of the hand?
questions.explain: Dorsal refers to the back of the hand and palmar refers to the palm of the hand, avoiding confusion with anterior and posterior when limb positions change. On the foot, the equivalent terms are dorsal and plantar.

open.q: Which two directional terms describe the back surface and palm surface of the hand?

questions.q: When describing structures on the sole of the foot regardless of foot position, which term is preferred over inferior?
questions.explain: Plantar specifically denotes the sole of the foot, whereas dorsal denotes the top (dorsum) of the foot. Rostral and cranial refer to headward directions.

open.q: Which directional term specifically describes the sole of the foot?

questions.q: Which term describes two structures that occur on the same side of the body?
questions.explain: Ipsilateral refers to structures on the same side of the body, such as the right thumb and right great toe. Contralateral refers to opposite sides of the body.

open.q: Which term describes structures located on the same side of the body?

questions.q: A patient has a stroke affecting the left motor cortex and develops weakness in the right arm. How is the right arm weakness described relative to the left brain lesion?
questions.explain: Contralateral means occurring on the opposite side of the body relative to another structure or lesion. Because most corticospinal fibers decussate in the medulla, a left cerebral lesion causes right-sided motor deficits.

open.q: A patient has a left cerebral hemisphere lesion causing weakness in the right upper limb. What term describes the relationship of the right limb weakness to the left brain lesion?

questions.q: Which term means situated closer to the head or upper end of the body?
questions.explain: Superior (or cranial) means nearer to the vertex or head end of the body. Inferior (or caudal) means nearer to the feet or tail end.

open.q: Which directional term means closer to the head or upper end of the body?

questions.q: Which directional term indicates a position closer to the surface of the body?
questions.explain: Superficial describes structures closer to the body surface, whereas deep (or profundus) describes structures farther from the surface.

open.q: Which directional term indicates a position closer to the surface of the body?

questions.q: Which movement bends a joint or decreases the angle between two bones in the sagittal plane?
questions.explain: Flexion generally decreases the angle between articulating bones and usually occurs in a sagittal plane. Extension straightens a joint and typically increases the angle between bones.

open.q: Which joint movement typically decreases the angle between articulating bones in a sagittal plane?

questions.q: Moving the arm away from the trunk in the coronal plane is called which movement?
questions.explain: Abduction moves a limb or digit away from the median plane or axial reference line in the coronal plane. Adduction moves it toward the median plane or midline of the hand/foot.

open.q: What is the movement of a limb away from the median plane of the body in the coronal plane?

questions.q: Which movement rotates the radius over the ulna so the palm of the hand faces posteriorly when starting from the anatomical position?
questions.explain: Pronation rotates the forearm and hand so the palm faces posteriorly (or inferiorly when the elbow is flexed). Supination turns the palm anteriorly or superiorly.

open.q: Which movement of the forearm rotates the radius across the ulna so the palm faces posteriorly from the anatomical position?

questions.q: Turning the sole of the foot away from the median plane (laterally) is known as which movement?
questions.explain: Eversion turns the plantar surface of the foot laterally away from the median plane, while inversion turns the sole medially toward the median plane.

open.q: What movement turns the sole of the foot laterally away from the median plane?

questions.q: A pianist brings the thumb across the palm to touch the tip of the little finger. Which specialized thumb movement is this?
questions.explain: Opposition brings the pad of the thumb into contact with the pad of another digit through combined flexion and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint. Reposition returns the thumb to its anatomical position.

open.q: What movement brings the pad of the thumb across the palm to touch another digit?

questions.q: Which movement of the foot raises the anterior part of the foot and toes toward the leg?
questions.explain: Dorsiflexion flexes the ankle joint so the dorsum of the foot moves superiorly toward the anterior leg. Plantarflexion depresses the toes and points the foot inferiorly.

open.q: Which ankle movement lifts the front of the foot and toes superiorly toward the leg?

questions.q: Which circular sequence combines flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction of a limb?
questions.explain: Circumduction is a sequential circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction so the distal end of the limb traces a circle. Rotation turns a limb or body part around its longitudinal axis.

open.q: Which movement combines flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction in sequence so a limb describes a cone?

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the face is directed:
questions.explain: The body stands erect with the face and eyes looking forward toward the horizon.

open.q: In the anatomical position, in which direction does the face look?

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the palms face:
questions.explain: The forearms are supinated so the palms face forward. Palms facing the thighs (medially) is the relaxed, non-standard position.

open.q: In the anatomical position, which direction do the palms face?

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the feet are:
options: Apart with the toes pointing laterally
Together with the toes pointing laterally
Together with the toes pointing forward
Apart with the toes pointing medially
questions.explain: The feet are placed together, flat on the ground, with the toes pointing forward.

open.q: Describe the position of the feet and toes in the anatomical position.
accept: Parallel with toes pointing to the front

questions.q: Which description of the upper limbs is correct for the anatomical position?
options: Raised above the head with the palms facing forward
Hanging by the sides with the palms facing backward
Hanging by the sides with the forearms supinated
questions.explain: The arms hang at the sides with the forearms supinated, so the palms and thumbs point forward and laterally.

open.q: How are the upper limbs positioned in the anatomical position?
accept: Arms by the sides with palms forward
Hanging at the sides with supinated forearms
Arms at the sides palms facing anteriorly

questions.q: What is the main purpose of describing the body in the anatomical position?
options: To provide a standard reference so descriptions are consistent
To place all muscles in a fully relaxed state
To show the body as it lies at birth
To place all joints in their loose-packed position
questions.explain: It is a conventional reference position, so relationships are described the same way whatever position the patient is actually in.

open.q: Why do anatomists describe all structures as if the body were in the anatomical position?

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into equal right and left halves?
questions.explain: The median (midsagittal) plane passes vertically through the midline from front to back. Coronal planes divide front from back.

open.q: What is the name of the vertical plane that passes through the midline and divides the body into equal right and left halves?

questions.q: A vertical plane at right angles to the median plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is the:
questions.explain: Coronal (frontal) planes run vertically from side to side. Sagittal planes run front to back.

open.q: What is the name of the vertical plane that divides the body into front and back parts?

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into superior and inferior parts at right angles to the long axis?
questions.explain: Transverse (horizontal or axial) planes cut across the body at right angles to the median and coronal planes.

open.q: What is the name of the plane that divides the body into upper and lower parts at right angles to its long axis?

questions.q: A vertical plane parallel to the median plane but not passing through the midline is called a:
questions.explain: Any vertical plane running front to back and parallel to the median plane is sagittal. Those off the midline are parasagittal.

open.q: What do we call a vertical anteroposterior plane that is parallel to, but away from, the median plane?

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the term cranial is equivalent to:
questions.explain: Cranial means toward the head, which in humans is superior. Caudal means toward the tail end, which is inferior.

open.q: In humans in the anatomical position, which direction does the term cranial describe?

questions.q: In human anatomy, the term ventral is equivalent to:
questions.explain: Ventral refers to the belly side, which is the front in humans. Dorsal refers to the back.

open.q: In human anatomy, which directional term is used interchangeably with ventral?

questions.q: Which term is equivalent to posterior in human anatomy?
questions.explain: Dorsal means toward the back. Caudal means toward the feet, which is inferior in humans.

open.q: Which directional term is used interchangeably with posterior in human anatomy?

questions.q: Relative to the eyes, the nose is:
questions.explain: Medial means nearer to the median plane. The nose lies closer to the midline than the eyes do.

open.q: What term describes a structure that is nearer to the median plane, such as the nose relative to the eyes?

questions.q: Which term means nearer to the attachment of a limb to the trunk, or nearer to the origin of a structure?
questions.explain: Proximal means closer to the point of attachment or origin. Distal means farther away.

open.q: What term describes a point nearer to the trunk end of a limb, such as the shoulder relative to the wrist?

questions.q: Which term describes a structure situated nearer to the surface of the body?
questions.explain: Superficial means closer to the body surface. Deep means farther from the surface.

open.q: What term describes a structure lying nearer to the surface of the body?

questions.q: Structures that are on the same side of the body are described as:
questions.explain: Ipsilateral means on the same side. Contralateral means on the opposite side, and bilateral means on both sides.

open.q: What term describes two structures lying on the same side of the body?

questions.q: The right hand and the left foot are described as being:
questions.explain: Structures on opposite sides of the body are contralateral. Ipsilateral and homolateral both mean the same side.

open.q: What term describes structures on opposite sides of the body, such as the right hand and the left foot?

questions.q: The anterior surface of the hand in the anatomical position is called the:
questions.explain: The palm is the palmar (volar) surface of the hand. The back of the hand is the dorsal surface.

open.q: What is the name of the anterior surface of the hand in the anatomical position?

questions.q: The inferior surface (sole) of the foot is called the:
questions.explain: The sole is the plantar surface. The upper surface of the foot is the dorsum.

open.q: What is the term for the surface of the sole of the foot?

questions.q: In the forearm in the anatomical position, the lateral (thumb) side is described as:
questions.explain: The radius lies on the thumb side, so the lateral side of the forearm is radial. The medial side is ulnar.

open.q: What adjective describes the thumb side of the forearm in the anatomical position?

questions.q: Which movement decreases the angle between two bones at a joint in the sagittal plane (for example at the elbow)?
questions.explain: Flexion bends a joint, usually in the sagittal plane. Extension straightens it.

open.q: What is the name of the movement that bends a joint and decreases the angle between the bones, such as at the elbow?

questions.q: Movement of a limb away from the median plane in the coronal plane is called:
questions.explain: Abduction moves a part away from the median plane. Adduction brings it back toward the plane.

open.q: What do we call movement of a limb away from the median plane, for example raising the arm out to the side?

questions.q: A circular movement made by sequential flexion, abduction, extension and adduction is called:
questions.explain: Circumduction combines movements in several planes so the distal end of the part traces a circle. The whole part sweeps a cone.

open.q: What is the name of the movement in which a limb traces a cone through sequential flexion, abduction, extension and adduction?

questions.q: Which forearm movement turns the palm to face posteriorly when starting from the anatomical position?
questions.explain: Pronation rotates the radius over the ulna so the palm faces backward. Supination returns the palm to face forward.

open.q: What do we call the forearm movement that turns the palm backward from the anatomical position?

questions.q: Which movement rotates the forearm so the palm faces forward in the anatomical position?
questions.explain: Supination turns the palm anteriorly and is the position of the forearm in the anatomical position. Pronation is the reverse.

open.q: What do we call the forearm movement that turns the palm forward?

questions.q: Turning the sole of the foot inward (medially) is called:
questions.explain: Inversion tilts the sole medially. Eversion turns it laterally.

open.q: What is the name of the movement that turns the sole of the foot medially?

questions.q: Which ankle movement raises the dorsum of the foot toward the shin?
questions.explain: Dorsiflexion decreases the angle between the foot and the leg. Plantarflexion points the toes downward.

open.q: What do we call the ankle movement that lifts the top of the foot toward the shin?

questions.q: Which movement brings the pad of the thumb across to touch the pads of the other fingers?
questions.explain: Opposition is the thumb movement that allows pinch and grip. It is a combination of flexion, abduction and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint.

open.q: What is the name of the thumb movement that brings its pad to touch the pads of the other fingers?

questions.q: Moving the mandible or the scapula forward on the body is called:
questions.explain: Protraction (protrusion) moves a part anteriorly. Retraction moves it back.

open.q: What do we call forward movement of a part such as the mandible or the scapula?

questions.q: Abduction and adduction of the fingers are defined relative to which digit?
questions.explain: The axis of the hand passes through the third digit, so spreading the fingers away from it is abduction and bringing them toward it is adduction.

open.q: Abduction and adduction of the fingers are measured relative to which digit?

questions.q: Abduction and adduction of the toes are defined relative to which toe?
questions.explain: The axis of the foot passes through the second toe. The great toe is not the reference.

open.q: Abduction and adduction of the toes are measured relative to which toe?

questions.q: A CT slice of the brain is viewed from below as if looking up from the patient's feet. In which anatomical plane does this slice lie?
questions.explain: A slice at right angles to the long axis of the body is transverse (axial). It is conventionally viewed from below with the patient's right side on the viewer's left.

open.q: A CT slice of the brain lies at right angles to the long axis of the body and is viewed from the patient's feet. In which anatomical plane is it?

questions.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and right leg only. The two affected limbs are described as being:
questions.explain: Both limbs are on the same side of the body, so they are ipsilateral. Contralateral would mean opposite sides.

open.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and right leg only. What term describes the relationship of these two limbs to each other?

questions.q: A patient lying face down on the examination couch is in which position?
questions.explain: Prone means lying face down. Supine means lying on the back, face up.

open.q: What is the name of the position of a patient lying face down?

questions.q: A patient lying on the back with the face directed upward is in which position?
questions.explain: Supine is lying on the back, face up. Trendelenburg is a tilted supine position with the head lower than the feet.

open.q: What is the name of the position of a patient lying flat on the back, face up?

questions.q: A laceration lies on the back of the forearm just above the wrist. Relative to the elbow, the laceration is:
questions.explain: The wrist is farther from the trunk than the elbow, so it is distal. The back of the forearm in the anatomical position is posterior (dorsal).

open.q: A laceration lies on the back of the forearm just higher than the wrist. Using two directional terms, describe its position relative to the elbow.

questions.q: After a nerve injury, a patient cannot bring the pad of the thumb to touch the pad of the little finger. Which thumb movement is lost?
questions.explain: Opposition combines flexion, abduction and medial rotation at the first carpometacarpal joint, bringing the thumb pad across to meet the other digits.

open.q: After a nerve injury, a patient cannot bring the pad of the thumb across to touch the pad of the little finger. Which thumb movement is lost?

questions.q: A footballer lands awkwardly and rolls the ankle so that the sole of the foot faces medially, stretching the lateral ligaments. Which movement has occurred?
questions.explain: Inversion turns the sole medially and is the usual mechanism of lateral ankle sprains. Eversion turns the sole laterally.

open.q: A footballer rolls the ankle so that the sole of the foot faces medially, stretching the lateral ligaments. Which movement of the foot has occurred?

questions.q: An MRI slice shows both cerebral hemispheres and both lateral ventricles, and it separates the front of the head from the back. In which plane was the slice taken?
questions.explain: A coronal slice runs vertically from side to side, so both hemispheres appear and the head is divided into anterior and posterior parts. Sagittal slices would show one half in profile.

open.q: An MRI slice shows both cerebral hemispheres and both lateral ventricles, and it divides the head into front and back parts. In which plane was the slice taken?

questions.q: For a pelvic examination, a patient lies on her back with the hips and knees flexed and the thighs abducted, with the feet in supports. Which position is this?
questions.explain: The lithotomy position exposes the perineum. Fowler is a semi-sitting position and Trendelenburg is a head-down tilt.

open.q: For a pelvic examination, a patient lies on her back with the hips and knees flexed, the thighs abducted and the feet in supports. What is this position called?

questions.q: A patient lies supine on a table that is tilted so the head is lower than the feet. Which position is this?
questions.explain: The Trendelenburg position is a supine head-down tilt. Fowler is the opposite, with the head and trunk raised.

open.q: A patient lies on the back on a table tilted so the head is lower than the feet. What is this position called?

questions.q: For a rectal examination, a patient lies on the left side with the right hip and knee flexed. Which position is this?
questions.explain: The left lateral or Sims position gives access to the anus and rectum. Lithotomy is on the back with the legs supported.

open.q: For a rectal examination, a patient lies on the left side with the right hip and knee flexed. What is this position called?

questions.q: A stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere causes weakness of the left arm. The weak arm is described as being what side relative to the lesion?
questions.explain: The weak arm is on the opposite side of the body from the lesion, so it is contralateral. Descending motor fibres cross over, which is why this happens.

open.q: A lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere causes weakness of the left arm. What term describes the side of the weak arm relative to the lesion?

questions.q: Relative to the heart, the sternum is:
questions.explain: The sternum lies in front of the heart and closer to the body surface. The vertebral column lies behind it.

open.q: Using two directional terms, describe the position of the sternum relative to the heart.
accept: In front and nearer the surface

questions.q: A waiter carries a tray of drinks balanced on an upturned palm. In which position is the forearm?
questions.explain: Supination turns the palm to face upward or forward. Pronation turns it downward or backward.

open.q: A waiter carries a tray balanced on an upturned palm. What name is given to this forearm position?

questions.q: A patient cannot raise the arm out to the side to shoulder height. Which movement at the shoulder is impaired?
questions.explain: Raising the arm sideways moves it away from the median plane in the coronal plane, which is abduction.

open.q: A patient cannot raise the arm out to the side to shoulder height. Which movement at the shoulder is impaired?
accept: Moving the arm away from the midline

questions.q: A ballet dancer rises onto her toes. Which movement occurs at the ankle?
questions.explain: Plantarflexion points the toes downward and raises the heel. Dorsiflexion is the opposite movement.

open.q: A ballet dancer rises onto her toes. What is the name of the movement at the ankle?

questions.q: Which plane of section would best show the nose, mouth and chin in profile?
questions.explain: A median sagittal section runs front to back through the midline, showing the facial profile and the nasal and oral cavities.

open.q: Which plane of section would best show the nose, mouth and chin in profile?

questions.q: Which statement uses anatomical terms incorrectly?
options: The elbow is proximal to the wrist.
The sternum is posterior to the vertebral column.
The skin is superficial to muscle.
The great toe is medial to the little toe.
questions.explain: The sternum lies on the front of the chest, so it is anterior to the vertebral column. The other three statements are correct.

questions.q: A patient has numbness along the ulnar border of the hand. Which digit lies on this side?
questions.explain: The ulna lies on the medial side of the forearm, so the ulnar border of the hand is the little finger side. The thumb is on the radial side.

open.q: A patient has numbness along the ulnar border of the hand. Which digit lies on this side?

questions.q: In the leg in the anatomical position, the fibula lies in which direction relative to the tibia?
questions.explain: The fibula is the slender bone on the lateral side of the leg. The tibia, which bears weight, is medial.

open.q: In the leg in the anatomical position, on which side of the tibia does the fibula lie?

questions.q: After a mandibular injury a patient cannot push the jaw forward. Which movement is impaired?
questions.explain: Protraction (protrusion) moves a part anteriorly. Retraction moves it back.

open.q: After a mandibular injury a patient cannot push the jaw forward. What is this movement called?

questions.q: A patient with a trapezius problem cannot shrug the shoulders. Which movement of the scapula is impaired?
questions.explain: Shrugging raises the scapula and shoulder girdle, which is elevation. Depression lowers them.

open.q: A patient cannot shrug the shoulders. Which movement of the scapula is impaired?

questions.q: A seated patient with the legs apart cannot bring the knees together against resistance. Which hip movement is weak?
questions.explain: Bringing the thighs toward the median plane is adduction. Moving them apart is abduction.

open.q: A seated patient with the legs apart cannot bring the knees together against resistance. Which hip movement is weak?

questions.q: Flexion and extension of the elbow occur mainly in which plane?
questions.explain: Flexion and extension are movements in the sagittal plane. Abduction and adduction occur in the coronal plane.

open.q: In which anatomical plane do flexion and extension of the elbow mainly occur?

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the middle finger lies between the index and ring fingers. Which term describes this relationship?
questions.explain: Intermediate describes a structure located between a more medial and a more lateral structure; the middle finger lies between the index and ring fingers.

open.q: Which anatomical term means situated between medial and lateral structures?

questions.q: A surgeon describes a section passing through the body at an angle to the standard sagittal, coronal and transverse planes. How is this section oriented?
questions.explain: An oblique section passes through the body at an angle rather than parallel or perpendicular to the standard anatomical planes.

open.q: What is a section made at an angle to the standard anatomical planes called?
